description: Hi! I’m a Diploma in Applied AI & Analytics student from Singapore Polytechnic, passionate about AI, data science, and solving real-world problems through technology. I have experience with Python, machine learning, data analytics, and web development. I’m joining NASA Space Apps to challenge myself, learn, and gain hackathon experience. I’m currently exploring Earth science data and climate trends, and I’m open to connecting with fellow participants who share similar interests!
summary: Both places warmed. Can you tell which warmed faster? Round Observatory turns that question into a field mission using NASA climate data. Students start with Singapore and Kuala Lumpur, make a prediction, then test their claim against 45 matched years of NASA POWER data. Both model grid points warmed, but the evidence does not establish which warmed faster. Students can send the same investigation to a partner class, change one setting, and exchange an Evidence Passport showing exactly what the data supports. A printable mission lets teachers run the activity even without a hosted app.
details:
Round Observatory is an interactive prototype for the “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge. The World Explorer lets users choose saved locations, a documented country or territory reference point, or custom coordinates. It retrieves gridded air temperature at 2 m (T2M) and relative humidity at 2 m (RH2M) from NASA POWER, based on MERRA-2. Users can visualize matched annual series, estimate rates per decade, test whether the trend gap differs from zero, and export their data sources and settings. Saved NASA responses allow the worked cases to run without a live NASA API connection.

The Singapore Field Mission holds Singapore fixed and lets students choose from six additional saved reference points, including Kuala Lumpur, Tokyo, and São Paulo. At the default grid points and 1981–2025 window, estimated temperature trends were +0.177 °C per decade near Singapore and +0.165 near Kuala Lumpur. The paired gap was +0.012 °C per decade (95% interval −0.011 to +0.035), so the exercise does not establish which warmed faster. Comparing predictions across two classrooms is a proposed use, not a tested adoption claim. Replay addresses encode a partner point, a variable, and a window without including predictions or student details. Both classrooms need access to the same hosted app for the link, or they can exchange the printable case offline.

In “Same Places, Different Story,” both model grid points near Tokyo and São Paulo warmed over 1981–2025. The Tokyo-minus-São Paulo temperature trend gap was −0.087 °C per decade (95% confidence interval −0.233 to +0.060). That interval does not establish which point warmed faster. Relative humidity rose by +0.577 percentage points per decade at the Tokyo point and fell by −1.817 at the São Paulo point. The paired humidity trend gap was +2.393 percentage points per decade (95% interval +1.677 to +3.110).

The regional lens asks a different question. If we replace the same single cells with two area-weighted 16-cell footprints, does the estimated temperature gap change? The paired shift was +0.088 °C per decade (95% interval +0.052 to +0.124), while both separate gap intervals included zero. This is evidence that the estimated gap changed with the spatial footprint in this case. It is not evidence that the sites traded places in a warming ranking. In the single-point view, students can compare monthly slopes, with Holm correction across 66 month pairs.

I built the prototype in Python with Streamlit and Plotly, used D3 for the interactive globe, and used pandas, NumPy, SciPy and statsmodels for data preparation and analysis. Matched trend gaps use ordinary least squares on annual paired differences, with Newey–West uncertainty and a check using an alternate lag. The Evidence Passport carries source URLs, checksums, settings, results and limitations. The worked cases were selected after exploration. These are fixed model grid cells and footprints, not city or country averages, forecasts, or causal claims.

ChatGPT (OpenAI) assisted with brainstorming, research, statistical interpretation, coding, debugging, visual design, documentation, and preparation of the demo. The final globe is rendered from Natural Earth map data. The app calculates its results from NASA POWER data using statistical code and does not run an AI model.
